title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
titleZh: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
author: rmason
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Emma Roth

comments.author: jjcm
comments.textRawHtml:
I work in the creative tools space.

This is one of the biggest issues right now. It's nearly impossible to separate "this image was fully generated with AI" versus "I made a minor edit to the colors or did a cutout or improved the layout with AI" when the endpoint is an image.

Especially for socials, if your brand is an authoritative source, getting hit with a dreaded "AI generated content" tag on instagram or facebook is a death blow to your credibility.

Design tools are in a very hard space because of it. You want to make edits as seamless as possible for users, but your final result can't include any pixels from a generative model. It's a strange dance.

children.author: dang
children.textRawHtml:
We're seeing this over and over in the text domain as well.

Users think they're using tools to "just" fix their grammar or polish their wording a bit, and don't realize that these leave almost as many imprints as copy-pasting everything from ChatGPT.

https://hn.algolia.com/?dateRange=all&page=0&prefix=true&que...

children.author: miki123211
children.textRawHtml:
Pangram (AI writing detector) is a lot more accurate than people think it is, but it measures something very different than what people think it measures.

Let's say two groups of people are writing scientific papers. The first is a group of native speakers of English who don't actually do any research, generate the paper from scratch, but then rewrite everything in their own words. They'll get a 0% (meaning human written) on Pangram.

Let's say the other group consists of non-native speakers of English who understand the language well, but are bad at writing in a style suitable for publication in a journal, so they write every paragraph in their own language and have AI translate. They've done all the research, they've had human authors understand and accept every single word of the paper, yet Pangram will tell them that the paper has been written by AI.

children.author: californical
children.textRawHtml:
Isn’t that what everyone thinks it measures? I think you make a very valid point about who is truly a more authoritative source, but I also don’t think anyone is confused about that.

I think in most contexts it would be extremely rare for somebody to rewrite the LLM output in their own words when they don’t know anything about a topic - especially because paraphrasing is really hard about a domain your unfamiliar with, and our human brains can pick up on those missing understandings

children.author: code51
children.textRawHtml: I see many academic reviewers do Pangram on top researchers' papers and if it comes out 100% AI, they declare the work AI slop. If you take any FAANG paper, chances are Pangram will give 100% for the paper. When there's blood, sweat, tears and real $$$ underneath.

children.author: addaon
children.textRawHtml:
> They've done all the research, they've had human authors understand and accept every single word of the paper, yet Pangram will tell them that the paper has been written by AI.

I don't think Pangram claims to provide any results about third-party understanding or "acceptance", though, do they? It's just about authorship. If I read an LLM generated document, even if I "accept" it, it can't possibly change that it was authored by an LLM, can it?

children.author: julian_t
children.textRawHtml:
If I get something I wrote translated into, say, French by a human translator, does that mean that they authored it? Seems to me that if the original thought is still there, the LLM did an equivalent translation job.

(And 'authored' is a horrible word. What's wrong with 'wrote'?)

children.author: shakna
children.textRawHtml:
> If I get something I wrote translated into, say, French by a human translator, does that mean that they authored it?

Well, that has been frequently argued in literary circles, since the first translation but... Generally speaking, today, yes.

They are given a lesser role to the original author, but are treated as an author, because of the choices that a translator must make. You'll find most "TA" or "Translator/Author"s get their name their on the translated work.

It isn't generally treated as literary appropriation - unless a word-by-word translation was done, in a mechanical manner or without acknowledging the original inspiration and source.

In such cases, which is roughly equivalent to the LLM there, it is treated as something that is opposed by the community, and has since before the printing press existed.

children.author: stackbutterflow
children.textRawHtml:
AI is breaking the chain of trust. We trust a human made translation.

Thinking about it using an LLM to translate or polish your text is like explaining your paper in great detail to someone and having this person produce a translated or polished text. For some reason we trust more a rewrite done by someone who's looking at the source material while doing it than someone who's listening to an explanation of it.
